title: These consultants are leaving the AI boom to protect the world from it
excerpt: Some consultants are uncomfortable with the industry's embrace of AI, and have left to help rein it in instead.
content_html:
Consultants have found an unlikely new career path: policing AI

By Lakshmi Varanasi

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

As consulting firms rapidly remake themselves to leverage AI, a small but growing number of consultants are leaving to rein it in.

Instead of joining the broader exodus to tech, these consultants are focusing on the risks that AI systems, from chatbots to agents, pose to society.

Namaan Mian, the chief operating officer of Management Consulted, a company that trains and prepares students and others for careers in consulting, said his firm has been tracking where former consultants land after leaving the industry. Roles in software development, operations at startups, IT, and, increasingly, venture capital and private equity remain primary destinations for former consultants, he said.

While moves into nonprofit and government roles, or smaller startups focused on regulating the technology, haven't appeared in the data yet, Mian said that "anecdotally," the field is gaining popularity.

Sarah Pomeranz, a former Accenture consultant, is now the founder and CEO of Consultants for Impact, a nonprofit that helps consultants transition into careers focused on pressing global problems. Pomeranz said that AI safety, governance, and policy accounted for roughly 4 in 10 of the high-impact career moves her organization has supported. That was about twice the share moving into global health and development, the next-largest category.

Pomeranz said former consultants have landed at organizations like the UK AI Safety Institute, RAND, European Union institutions, and policy teams at frontier AI labs.

"A lot of these ex-BCG and McKinsey consultants are staffing the institutions that are, in many ways, governing," she said.

The consultants who have made the leap

Business Insider spoke to former consultants who left consulting to take up roles at AI safety nonprofits, policy organizations, government roles, and research institutes. They've helped governments design AI rules and managed researchers studying how advanced systems could cause catastrophic harm.

"There's more and more of a need for generalists — just really good operators who actually know how to run an organization, make it grow, have good management practices," said Lucas Le Merlus Schmuck, a former Bain consultant who now works on the technical AI safety team at the nonprofit Coefficient Giving.

Schmuck, who spent a year and a half at Bain before pursuing a master's degree in public policy focused on AI governance, said moving directly from consulting into an AI safety nonprofit remains relatively rare. He said consultants generally need to first build familiarity with the field through courses and independent research.

"You usually need to acquire a little more context about the space," he said. "You want to make sure that people are mission-aligned with what the organization wants to do."

Peter Wallich, a former BCG consultant, now works as a senior research program manager at the Constellation Institute, where one of his tasks is to help run programs to bring more researchers into AI safety. The role involves a mix of management and coaching — a natural fit, he said, for the skills he developed in consulting.

He said BCG had been valuable early in his career, but he believed consulting firms had underestimated both AI's transformative potential and its most severe risks.

"I wish that they took a more proactive stance on risks that they don't have strong commercial incentives to work against," he said. "I don't have ill will for the firm, and I am grateful for my experience."

The ratio of people pushing for returns from AI still vastly outnumbers those working on its potential for harm. For "every hundred people that are trying to push the frontier, trying to build AI that can outperform humans, there is one person trying to prevent catastrophes resulting from that," Wallich said.

But those working on AI safety say they increasingly encounter former colleagues who have made the switch.

David Conrad, who worked at BCG in Australia, said he first entered consulting because he was unsure what he wanted to do and saw the firm as a professional "finishing school." Now, he runs a nonprofit that trains people for AI policy and governance jobs across Europe.

"It definitely feels like I very regularly come across consultants in AI safety and AI policy," he said. "It feels that there's a disproportionate number of consultants here."

AI safety organizations compete with well-funded labs for technical talent, so salaries can be unusually high for the nonprofit sector, Schmuck said. The trade-off is probably more significant for principals and partners.

"If you exit at a consultant or associate consultant level, sometimes it's not even a pay cut," Schmuck said. "Sometimes it's the same or a pay bump."

Pomeranz also said that AI may be making traditionally secure paths feel less certain. As firms freeze hiring, cut roles, and automate more junior work, joining a nonprofit, startup, or smaller organization may no longer seem like a leap into uncharted waters.

"It changes the calculus when the safe options are also not sure things," she said.

顾问们发现了一条不太可能的新职业道路：监管人工智能

作者：Lakshmi Varanasi 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

随着咨询公司迅速重塑自身以利用人工智能，一小部分但越来越多的顾问正在离开以控制人工智能。

这些顾问没有加入更广泛的科技浪潮，而是关注人工智能系统（从聊天机器人到代理）给社会带来的风险。

Management Consulted 是一家为学生和其他人从事咨询职业提供培训和准备的公司，其首席运营官纳马安·米安 (Namaan Mian) 表示，他的公司一直在追踪前咨询顾问在离开该行业后的去向。 他表示，软件开发、初创公司运营、IT 以及越来越多的风险投资和私募股权领域的职位仍然是前顾问的主要目的地。

虽然数据中还没有出现进入非营利组织和政府角色，或专注于监管技术的小型初创公司，但米安表示，“据传闻”，该领域正在变得越来越受欢迎。

莎拉·波梅兰兹 (Sarah Pomeranz) 曾是埃森哲 (Accenture) 顾问，现在是 Consultants for Impact 的创始人兼首席执行官，这是一个非营利组织，帮助顾问过渡到专注于解决紧迫的全球问题的职业。 Pomeranz 表示，在她的组织支持的高影响力职业变动中，人工智能安全、治理和政策约占十分之四。 这大约是第二大类别全球健康与发展领域份额的两倍。

波慕兰表示，前顾问已进入英国人工智能安全研究所、兰德公司、欧盟机构和前沿人工智能实验室政策团队等组织。

“许多前 BCG 和麦肯锡顾问都在为在很多方面进行管理的机构工作，”她说。

实现飞跃的顾问

《商业内幕》采访了一些前顾问，他们离开咨询行业，在人工智能安全非营利组织、政策组织、政府和研究机构任职。 他们帮助政府设计人工智能规则，并管理研究人员研究先进系统如何造成灾难性伤害。

贝恩前顾问、现供职于非营利组织 Coefficient Giving 的技术人工智能安全团队的卢卡斯·勒·梅鲁斯·施穆克 (Lucas Le Merlus Schmuck) 表示：“人们越来越需要多面手——真正优秀的运营商，他们真正知道如何运营一个组织，使其成长，拥有良好的管理实践。”

施穆克在贝恩公司工作了一年半，然后攻读了专注于人工智能治理的公共政策硕士学位，他表示，直接从咨询转向人工智能安全非营利组织的情况仍然相对较少。 他说，顾问通常需要首先通过课程和独立研究来熟悉该领域。

“你通常需要了解更多有关该空间的背景信息，”他说。 “你要确保人们的使命与组织想要做的事情保持一致。”

Peter Wallich 是前 BCG 顾问，现在担任星座研究所的高级研究项目经理，他的任务之一是帮助运行项目，让更多研究人员进入人工智能安全领域。 他说，这个角色涉及管理和辅导的结合，这对于他在咨询中培养的技能来说是很自然的选择。

他表示，BCG 在他职业生涯的早期就很有价值，但他认为咨询公司低估了人工智能的变革潜力及其最严重的风险。

他说：“我希望他们对风险采取更积极主动的立场，因为他们没有强大的商业动机来应对这些风险。” “我对公司没有恶意，我很感激我的经历。”

追求人工智能回报的人数仍然远远多于致力于人工智能潜在危害的人数。 沃利奇说，“每一百个人试图推动前沿，试图构建能够超越人类的人工智能，就有一个人试图防止由此引发的灾难。”

但那些从事人工智能安全工作的人表示，他们越来越多地遇到已经做出转变的前同事。

在澳大利亚 BCG 工作的戴维·康拉德 (David Conrad) 表示，他最初进入咨询行业是因为不确定自己想做什么，并将该公司视为专业的“精修学校”。 现在，他经营着一家非营利组织，为整个欧洲的人工智能政策和治理工作人员提供培训。

“我确实感觉自己经常遇到人工智能安全和人工智能政策方面的顾问，”他说。 “感觉这里的顾问数量不成比例。”

施穆克说，人工智能安全组织与资金雄厚的实验室争夺技术人才，因此非营利部门的薪水可能异常高。 对于委托人和合伙人来说，这种权衡可能更为重要。

“如果你在顾问或副顾问级别退出，有时甚至不会减薪，”施穆克说。 “有时工资是一样的，或者是加薪。”

彭慕兰还表示，人工智能可能会让传统的安全路径变得不那么确定。 随着公司冻结招聘、裁员并自动化更多初级工作，加入非营利组织、初创公司或小型组织似乎不再像是进入未知领域。

“当安全选择也不确定时，它就会改变计算方式，”她说。
